questions.q: CQS vs CQRS: what is each, what read/write mismatch does CQRS address, and what does it cost?
questions.a:
### CQS (Bertrand Meyer)
A **method** either changes state (command) or returns data (query), never both. A design principle at the method level.

### CQRS (Greg Young)
Applies the idea at the **architecture** level: separate **models** (and possibly stores) for **writes** and **reads**.
- **Write side**: commands handled by aggregates that enforce invariants; normalised, consistency-focused.
- **Read side**: queries served from **read models** shaped for each screen or API; denormalised, query-focused.

### The mismatch
| Writes need | Reads need |
|---|---|
| invariants, transactions, small aggregates | joins across aggregates, filters, sorting, paging, aggregations |
| normalised data | denormalised, pre-computed views |
| low volume, strict consistency | high volume (often 10 to 100 times writes), tolerance for slight staleness |
| one model | many shapes (list, detail, dashboard, search, export) |
One model serving both ends up bent: aggregates exposing collections for screens, queries loading whole aggregates, indexes fighting writes.

### Costs
Synchronising the read side (often eventually consistent), more moving parts (projectors, stores), duplicated data, rebuild tooling, and UI handling of lag. Start with the cheapest level that solves the problem.
questions.dia:
flowchart LR
  UI[Client] -->|commands| CH[Command handlers]
  CH --> AG[Aggregates enforce invariants]
  AG --> WDB[(Write store)]
  WDB -->|events or changes| PR[Projectors]
  PR --> RDB[(Read models)]
  UI -->|queries| QH[Query handlers]
  QH --> RDB
pts: CQS separates commands and queries at method level; CQRS at model level.
Writes need invariants; reads need many denormalised shapes.
One model serving both gets bent in both directions.
Costs: synchronisation, eventual consistency, moving parts.
Use the cheapest level that solves the problem.
questions.ex: A lending platform's Loan aggregate had grown navigation properties and computed fields for 14 screens; saving a loan loaded 9 tables. Moving screens to read models shrank the aggregate to its invariants and cut save latency by 80%.

questions.q: Describe the three practical levels of CQRS (separate code paths, separate read tables, separate read stores), their consistency and complexity, and how you choose.
questions.a:
| Level | Write side | Read side | Consistency | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Separate code paths** | aggregates (EF Core) | query handlers projecting from the **same database** (EF {{Select}}, Dapper, views) | immediate | low: use almost everywhere |
| **2. Separate read tables, same database** | aggregates | denormalised tables or materialised/indexed views updated **in the same transaction** or right after | immediate or near-real-time | medium |
| **3. Separate read stores** | aggregates (± event sourcing) | Elasticsearch, Redis, Cosmos DB, another SQL database, updated by **projectors consuming events** | **eventual** | high |

### Choosing
1. Start at level 1: separate query code, projections, indexes.
2. Move to level 2 when queries remain too slow or complex despite indexes (many joins, aggregations computed on every request).
3. Move to level 3 when read load must scale independently, a different technology is needed (full-text search, key-value at huge scale), or other contexts need the data, **and** the business accepts a measured lag.

### Rules
Mix levels per read model; the choice is local, not system-wide. Each step up adds operational cost (projectors, monitoring, rebuilds).
pts: Level 1: separate query code on the same database; immediate.
Level 2: denormalised tables in the same database; immediate or near-real-time.
Level 3: separate stores via projectors; eventual.
Start at level 1; escalate per read model with evidence.
Each level adds operational cost.
questions.ex: A team jumped straight to level 3 with Kafka and Elasticsearch for a back-office with 50 users; projection lag bugs consumed a quarter. Dropping to level 1 for most screens and keeping Elasticsearch only for free-text search simplified operations dramatically.

Can level 2 be eventually consistent?

questions.q: Commands, queries and events: how do they differ in intent, naming, ownership and handling? Can a command return data, and can a command be rejected?
questions.a:
| | Command | Query | Event |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intent | ask the system to **do** something | ask for **information** | announce that something **happened** |
| Naming | imperative: {{ApproveLoan}}, {{CapturePayment}} | {{GetLoanSummary}}, {{SearchPayments}} | past tense: {{LoanApproved}} |
| Handlers | exactly **one** | exactly one | **zero to many** subscribers |
| Can fail / be rejected | **yes** (validation, invariants, authorization) | yes (not found, forbidden) | no: it is a fact |
| Side effects | changes state | none | triggers reactions in subscribers |
| Owner | the receiving context | the receiving context | the publishing context |

### Can a command return data?
Strict CQS says no. Pragmatically, return **minimal** information: success/failure with reason, the new **id**, the new **version** (for concurrency or read-your-own-writes). Do not return read models: that couples the command side to screen shapes.

### Commands carry intent
{{ChangeCustomerAddress(reason: Moved)}} is better than {{UpdateCustomer(dto)}}: the business meaning lets the aggregate apply the right rules and produce meaningful events ({{CustomerMoved}} vs {{AddressCorrected}}).

### Identity
Commands carry a **command id** for idempotency; events carry an **event id**, the aggregate id and version, and causation/correlation ids linking them to the command.
pts: Commands ask (can be rejected), queries read, events state facts.
Imperative command names; past-tense events.
One handler per command or query; many subscribers per event.
Commands return minimal data: status, id, version.
Commands carry intent; ids enable idempotency and tracing.
questions.ex: An UpdateCustomer(dto) endpoint produced a generic CustomerUpdated event; the AML team could not tell relocations (risk-relevant) from typo corrections. Intent-specific commands and events let compliance trigger reviews only for real moves.

questions.q: Clear up common CQRS misconceptions: CQRS vs event sourcing, CQRS vs MediatR, CQRS vs microservices, and "CQRS means two databases".
questions.a:
| Misconception | Reality |
|---|---|
| "CQRS requires event sourcing" | Independent. CQRS separates read and write models; event sourcing stores state as events. ES pairs naturally with CQRS (you need projections to query an event store), but CQRS works with ordinary state-based persistence. |
| "Using MediatR with Command and Query classes is CQRS" | MediatR is an in-process dispatcher. Naming requests "commands" and "queries" while both go through the same aggregates and repositories is not CQRS; separate **models** is the point. |
| "CQRS means two databases" | Level 1 uses one database with separate code paths; separate stores are an option, not a requirement. |
| "CQRS means eventual consistency" | Only when read models are updated asynchronously (level 3). Levels 1 and 2 can be immediately consistent. |
| "CQRS is a system architecture" | It is usually applied **within a bounded context**, to specific parts with read/write mismatch, not across a whole system. |
| "CQRS requires microservices" | No; it works in a single deployable. |

### What CQRS actually is
A decision to give reads and writes **different models** because they have different needs, with a chosen synchronisation mechanism.
pts: CQRS and event sourcing are independent but complementary.
A mediator with Command/Query names is not CQRS.
One database is fine; separate stores are optional.
Eventual consistency only with asynchronous projections.
Apply within a bounded context where reads and writes mismatch.
questions.ex: A team proudly reported "full CQRS" because every endpoint used MediatR commands and queries; all queries loaded aggregates and the read performance problems remained. Introducing actual read models for the three slow screens fixed performance without touching MediatR.

questions.q: What is a read model, how do you design one per screen or API, and why is denormalisation acceptable on the read side?
questions.a:
### Definition
A **read model** is data shaped for a specific query use: a list screen, a detail page, a dashboard tile, a search index, an API response. It is derived from the write side (directly, via tables updated alongside, or via events) and contains **no business rules for changing state**.

### Design per use case
- Start from the **consumer**: what does the screen show, filter, sort and page by?
- Include **pre-joined** fields (customer name next to loan amount) and **pre-computed** values (outstanding balance, days overdue) where computing them per request is expensive.
- Key and index by the access pattern (merchant + date, account + booking date).
- Keep **ids and versions** of source entities for idempotent updates and linking back.

### Why denormalisation is fine
The write side remains the **source of truth** with invariants. Read models are **derived and disposable**: they can be rebuilt. Duplication is a deliberate trade for fast, simple reads. The risks are staleness and inconsistency between read models, managed by projection design and monitoring.

### Smells
- One generic read model mirroring the domain (just a copy of the write tables).
- Read models with update logic beyond applying events (business rules leaking).
- Read models queried to make write decisions.
pts: Read models are derived data shaped for one query use.
Design from the consumer: show, filter, sort, page.
Pre-join and pre-compute expensive values; index by access pattern.
Denormalisation is fine because read models are disposable and rebuildable.
Never make write decisions from read models.
questions.ex: A merchant portal computed refunded amounts and customer names by joining five tables per row; at 30 merchants per second it saturated the database. A per-screen read model with those values pre-computed served the same page in 5 ms.
fu: How many read models is too many?

pit: Generic mirrors of the write model.

questions.q: What does eventual consistency mean for a CQRS read side in practice: what can users observe, how is lag measured, and which decisions must never be made on eventually consistent data?
questions.a:
### Definition
After a command commits, read models reflect it **after a delay** (milliseconds to seconds, longer under load or failure). Given no new writes, all read models converge.

### What users can observe
- **Stale reads**: the list still shows the old status right after saving.
- **Read models disagreeing**: the dashboard total updated, the list not yet.
- **Out-of-order effects** if projections are badly designed (newer state overwritten by older).

### Measuring lag
- **Time lag**: now minus the occurred-at time of the last event applied, per projection.
- **Position lag**: events behind the head of the stream/partition (consumer lag).
- Publish both as metrics; define an **SLO** ("99% of updates visible within 2 seconds") and alert on breach.

### Never decide on eventually consistent data
- Balance checks, credit limits, stock reservations, duplicate checks, authorisation decisions: use the **write side** (authoritative, consistent).
- Read models are for **display, search, reporting**.

### Design for it
UI patterns (optimistic updates, pending markers, read-your-own-writes), clear communication of "as of" times on dashboards, and degradations when lag exceeds thresholds.
pts: Read models converge after a delay; users may see stale or disagreeing views.
Measure time lag and position lag; define an SLO and alert.
Never base money, limits or duplicates decisions on read models.
Read models serve display, search and reporting.
Show "as of" times and handle lag in the UI.
questions.ex: A payout feature checked the merchant's available balance from a dashboard read model; during a projection backlog it paid out 1.2 million GBP against balances that had already been reduced by chargebacks. Moving the check to the write-side balance aggregate closed the hole.

pit: Pretending the read side is immediately consistent.

questions.q: Write a production-grade command handler in .NET for the CQRS write side: validation, loading the aggregate, invariants, concurrency, idempotency, events via outbox, and the result returned.
questions.a:
### Steps
1. **Validate** the command's shape (pipeline/validator) before touching data.
2. **Idempotency**: if the command id was already processed, return the stored result.
3. **Load** the aggregate through its repository (tracked), with its version.
4. **Authorise** against the loaded resource.
5. **Execute** domain behaviour; invariants enforced by the aggregate; domain events raised.
6. **Persist** in one transaction: aggregate changes, outbox rows (integration events), idempotency record.
7. **Return** a minimal result: success/error code, id, new version.

### Concurrency
Expected version from the client (for edits based on what the user saw) or optimistic concurrency with retry of the whole handler for system commands.

### What does not belong
Read-model updates (those come from projections), external calls inside the transaction, returning view DTOs.
pts: Validate, check idempotency, load, authorise, execute, persist, return minimal result.
Aggregate changes, outbox and idempotency record in one transaction.
Expected version for user edits; whole-handler retries for system commands.
No read-model updates or external calls inside the handler's transaction.
Return status, id and version, not views.
questions.ex: A loan approval endpoint double-approved loans when users double-clicked; each approval emitted a LoanApproved event and downstream disbursement ran twice. Command ids with an idempotency record in the same transaction stopped duplicates.
fu: Where is the idempotency record stored and for how long?
How do you return validation errors for multiple fields?
What if the command needs data from another context?
pit: Updating read models in the command handler.

questions.q: Write efficient query handlers for the read side: EF Core projections vs Dapper vs SQL views, pagination, filtering, authorization filters, and caching.
questions.a:
### Data access options
| Option | Use |
|---|---|
| EF Core {{AsNoTracking}} + {{Select}} into DTOs | most queries; type-safe, composable |
| Dapper / raw SQL | complex reporting SQL, window functions, hints, maximum control |
| SQL views / indexed (materialised) views | reused complex joins, level-2 read models |
| Dedicated read stores | search, key-value, documents |

### Rules
- **Never** load aggregates; project only needed columns.
- **Keyset pagination** for large lists; total counts only when needed (or approximate).
- **Authorization filters** (tenant, owner, permissions) applied in every query, ideally centrally (base query, global filters, RLS).
- Validate filter and sort inputs (allow-lists) for dynamic queries.
- **Caching** for expensive, hot, slowly changing queries, keyed by user/tenant scope, invalidated by events or short TTLs.
- Separate connection pool or read replica for heavy reporting queries so they do not starve OLTP.

### Shape
Query objects/handlers per use case returning DTOs designed for the consumer; no business rules; side-effect free.
pts: Projections, Dapper, views or read stores per need; never aggregates.
Keyset pagination; counts only when needed.
Authorization filters in every query, centrally where possible.
Allow-list dynamic filters and sorts; cache hot, slow-changing queries.
Heavy reporting on replicas or separate pools.
questions.ex: A merchant search endpoint filtered by tenant in the controller but one new query handler forgot it, exposing other merchants' payments in a search result. Moving the tenant filter into a base query (plus RLS in the database) made the omission impossible.

questions.q: Design a projector that keeps a read model up to date from events: event sources (outbox stream, event store, CDC), handler structure, upserts, and how one projector handles several event types.
questions.a:
### Sources
- **Outbox → broker** (Kafka, Service Bus): integration events, the common choice across services.
- **Event store subscriptions** (EventStoreDB, Marten): when the write side is event-sourced.
- **CDC** (Debezium) on write tables: when the write side does not publish events; couples projections to table structure.

### Structure
- One projector per read model (or a small group of related read models), **independent consumer group** per projector.
- A handler per event type that **upserts** the view row(s) keyed by entity id.
- Each view row stores the **source version**; checkpoint/offset stored with the update.
- Projectors contain **mapping only**: no business decisions, no calls to other services in the hot path (enrich via events or local reference tables).

### Several event types
Events for one entity ({{PaymentAuthorised}}, {{PaymentCaptured}}, {{PaymentRefunded}}) all upsert the same row; each sets the fields it knows. A missing row on a later event (because an earlier event was lost or is out of order) is handled explicitly (create a partial row, park, or fetch).

### Performance
Batch writes (process 100 to 1,000 events per transaction), bulk upserts, partition parallelism.
pts: Sources: outbox stream, event store subscriptions or CDC.
One projector per read model, independent consumer group.
Upserts keyed by entity id with source versions.
Mapping only; no business decisions or remote calls.
Batch writes and partition parallelism for throughput.
questions.ex: A dashboard projector called the customer service for every event to enrich names; when that service slowed, projection lag reached 40 minutes. Consuming CustomerRenamed events into a local lookup table removed the remote call and lag stayed under a second.
fu: When is CDC a better projection source than events?
How do you handle an event for a row that does not exist yet?
How large should projection batches be?
pit: One consumer group shared by several projectors.

questions.q: Why must projections be idempotent, and how do you make different kinds of projections idempotent (state rows, counters/aggregates, append-only lists)?
questions.a:
### Why
Delivery is **at least once**: relays and brokers redeliver after crashes and rebalances; rebuilds replay history. Without idempotency, counters double, totals drift, newer state is overwritten by older.

### Techniques by projection kind
| Projection | Technique |
|---|---|
| **State row per entity** (status, latest values) | store the source **version**; apply only if newer (or exactly next); upsert by id |
| **Counters / aggregates** (daily totals) | record processed **event ids** in the same transaction (dedupe table per projection), or recompute from source rows, or make increments keyed (insert-if-absent per event) |
| **Append-only lists** (timelines, statements) | unique constraint on event id; insert-if-not-exists |
| **Search documents** | index with version-based external versioning (Elasticsearch {{version_type=external}}) |

### Checkpoint atomicity
Store the checkpoint (offset/position) in the **same transaction** as the read-model change. If they are in different stores, rely on per-event idempotency as above.

### Dedupe table hygiene
Keep processed ids for at least the redelivery window (or forever with compact storage if rebuilds replay from the start, in which case truncate the projection and dedupe table together).
pts: At-least-once delivery and replays require idempotent projections.
State rows: version check and upsert.
Counters: processed-event dedupe in the same transaction.
Lists: unique event ids; search: external versioning.
Checkpoint atomically with updates, or rely on per-event idempotency.
questions.ex: A daily-revenue projection double-counted after every Kafka rebalance; finance noticed totals 0.3% above the ledger. A processed-events table in the same transaction made totals match the ledger exactly.

questions.q: How do you guarantee per-entity ordering in projections, detect gaps, and handle out-of-order or missing events without blocking every other entity?
questions.a:
### Ordering
- Publish events with the **entity (aggregate) id as the partition key**: a broker partition preserves order per key.
- One consumer processes a partition sequentially (or uses per-key lanes inside the consumer).
- Events carry the **aggregate version** (1, 2, 3...).

### Applying
- {{version <= stored}}: duplicate or stale → skip.
- {{version == stored + 1}}: apply.
- {{version > stored + 1}}: **gap** (an earlier event missing or delayed).

### Handling gaps
- **Retry with backoff** for a short time (the earlier event may be in flight on another partition after a key change, or in a retry queue).
- **Park** the event in a per-entity holding table and continue with other entities; re-process when the missing event arrives.
- **Self-heal**: fetch the current state of the entity from the write side (an API or snapshot) and rebuild that row.
- Alert if gaps persist.

### Do not
Block the whole partition for one entity's gap (head-of-line blocking) beyond a short retry; or skip gaps silently (permanent wrong data).

### Cross-entity ordering
Not guaranteed and usually not needed; if a read model combines entities, design it to tolerate arbitrary interleaving.
pts: Partition by entity id; process each partition in order.
Events carry aggregate versions; apply only the next version.
Gaps: short retry, park per entity, self-heal from the source.
Avoid head-of-line blocking and silent skips.
Design combined read models to tolerate cross-entity interleaving.
questions.ex: A projection silently skipped versions it considered "missing"; after a broker failover, 1,800 accounts showed wrong statuses for days. Parking with self-healing from the write side corrected them within minutes and an alert now fires on persistent gaps.
fu: What happens when the partition key changes?
How do you rebuild a single entity's row?
How long should you wait before self-healing?
pit: Blocking a whole partition on one entity.

questions.q: Where should a projector store its checkpoint (offset/position), and how do you get exactly-once effects when the source is Kafka and the read store is SQL, Elasticsearch or Redis?
questions.a:
### The problem
A projector reads event N, updates the read model, then records "processed N". A crash between the two steps leads to either reprocessing (if the checkpoint is saved after) or skipping (if saved before).

### SQL read store
Store the **checkpoint in the same database transaction** as the read-model update (a {{ProjectionCheckpoints}} table keyed by projection and partition). On startup, the projector **seeks** the Kafka consumer to the stored offsets instead of using Kafka's committed offsets. Result: exactly-once effect.

### Stores without multi-item transactions (Elasticsearch, Redis)
- Make each write **idempotent** (version-based or id-based) so reprocessing is harmless.
- Commit offsets to Kafka **after** writes are acknowledged.
- Optionally store checkpoints in the same store with conditional writes, but rely primarily on idempotency.

### Event stores
Subscriptions provide positions; persist the position with the read model (same transaction) or rely on idempotent writes.

### Batching
Process a batch, write rows and the checkpoint in one transaction, commit. Large batches improve throughput but increase reprocessing after a crash; tune.

### Rule of thumb
Never trust "exactly-once delivery" claims across systems; build **idempotent effects** and keep checkpoints atomic where you can.
pts: Checkpoint and update must not be separable by a crash.
SQL: store checkpoints in the same transaction; seek on startup.
Non-transactional stores: idempotent writes, commit offsets after acks.
Batch with atomic checkpoint per batch; tune batch size.
Build idempotent effects; do not rely on exactly-once delivery.
questions.ex: A projector committed Kafka offsets before writing to SQL; a pod OOM-kill lost 12,000 events from a statements read model, discovered by customers. Moving checkpoints into the SQL transaction and seeking on startup made restarts lossless.

What batch size would you start with?
How does Kafka transactional produce/consume fit in?

questions.q: A user saves a change and the list still shows the old data. Design read-your-own-writes and other UX patterns for eventually consistent read models, for both Angular/React front ends and APIs.
questions.a:
### Patterns
1. **Optimistic UI**: apply the change locally from the command's success response; reconcile when fresh data arrives.
2. **Return the version** from the command; the client (or API) **waits** for the read model to reach that version (bounded, e.g. 2 seconds), then reads.
3. **Read the user's own item from the write side** for the detail view immediately after a change; lists can lag.
4. **Pending markers**: show "processing" for items the user just changed until the projection catches up.
5. **Push notifications** (SignalR/WebSockets/SSE) when a projection updates entities the user is viewing.
6. **Session stickiness**: a per-session "last written version" header that query endpoints honour (wait or fall back).

### API design
- Commands return {{version}} and a {{Location}} to the resource.
- Query endpoints accept {{minVersion}} (or an {{If-None-Match}}-style header) and either wait briefly or return 202/409 with retry guidance.

### Choosing
Combine: optimistic UI for responsiveness, version-wait for correctness on critical screens, push for collaboration features. Measure lag so the wait window is realistic.
pts: Optimistic UI from command responses.
Return versions; wait briefly for the read model to reach them.
Read the user's own item from the write side when needed.
Pending markers and push notifications for updates.
Size waits from measured lag.
questions.ex: Underwriters approved loans and immediately saw them still "Pending" in the queue, so they approved again, creating duplicate tasks. Optimistic updates plus a version wait on the queue refresh removed the confusion and the duplicate approvals.

When is push better than polling?

questions.q: Choose read-store technologies for different read models: relational, search engine, key-value cache, document store, analytics warehouse. What criteria decide, and what does each cost operationally?
questions.a:
| Need | Store | Strengths | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| lists, filters, joins, reports | **SQL** (denormalised tables, indexed views) | familiar, transactional, rich queries | scaling writes and huge datasets |
| full-text, fuzzy, faceted search | **Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Azure AI Search** | relevance, facets, aggregations | cluster operations, reindexing, eventual consistency |
| key lookups at very high rate | **Redis, DynamoDB, Cosmos DB** | microsecond to millisecond reads, scale-out | limited querying, memory cost (Redis) |
| per-screen documents | **MongoDB/Cosmos DB** | one read per screen, flexible shape | duplication, cross-document queries |
| analytics, large aggregations | **warehouse/lakehouse** (Snowflake, Databricks, Synapse, BigQuery) | massive scans, BI tools | latency minutes, cost per query |
| graph traversals | Neo4j, Gremlin | relationships | niche skills |

### Criteria
Query patterns, latency targets, data volume, consistency window, retention and compliance (data residency, immutability), team skills, and **operational cost** (each new store needs backups, monitoring, upgrades, security, on-call knowledge).

### Advice
Prefer the stores you already operate; add a new technology only for a capability you cannot reasonably get otherwise (full-text search is the common one). One read model may feed several stores from the same events.
pts: Match the store to the query pattern: SQL, search, key-value, documents, warehouse.
Weigh latency, volume, consistency window, retention, skills.
Every new store adds operational cost.
Prefer stores you already run; add new ones for real capabilities.
The same events can feed several stores.
questions.ex: A team added MongoDB, Redis and Elasticsearch for one service's read models; on-call engineers struggled with three unfamiliar stores during an incident. Consolidating to SQL plus Elasticsearch for search reduced incidents and kept performance targets.

When is Redis a bad read store?

questions.q: Level-2 CQRS inside one database: synchronous projections in the same transaction, indexed/materialised views, and summary tables. When is this better than asynchronous projections, and what are the costs?
questions.a:
### Options
| Option | How | Consistency | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Synchronous projection** in the same transaction (interceptor or handler updates read tables) | read rows updated with the write | immediate | longer write transactions; contention on hot summary rows |
| **SQL Server indexed views** | engine maintains the view on every write | immediate | write overhead, strict requirements (schemabinding, deterministic functions), hot-row contention |
| **PostgreSQL materialised views** | refreshed on demand ({{REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY}}) | stale until refresh | refresh cost; scheduling |
| **Summary tables updated by background jobs** | periodic recomputation | stale by schedule | job management |

### Better than asynchronous projections when
- The read model lives in the same database and the business needs **immediate** consistency (operational screens, approval queues).
- Volumes are moderate; no need for a separate store.
- The team wants CQRS benefits without brokers and projector infrastructure.

### Watch out for
- **Hot rows**: a daily total per merchant updated by every payment serialises writes (shard the counter or aggregate asynchronously).
- Transaction size growth.
- Coupling read-model schema changes to write deployments.
pts: Synchronous projections and indexed views give immediate consistency in one database.
Materialised views and summary jobs are stale until refresh.
Choose when immediacy matters and volumes are moderate.
Watch hot summary rows and transaction growth.
No broker or projector infrastructure needed.
questions.ex: An underwriting team needed the approval queue to reflect decisions instantly; asynchronous projections caused duplicate work. A synchronous queue projection in the same transaction fixed it with no new infrastructure.

What are SQL Server indexed view restrictions?

pit: Indexed views on very hot tables.

questions.q: Command design for reliability: command ids, idempotency storage, validation layers, expected versions, and returning useful errors to clients.
questions.a:
### Command id
Client-generated (UUID) per user intent; retries reuse it. Over HTTP it maps to an {{Idempotency-Key}} header; over messaging to the message id or a business key.

### Idempotency storage
A table keyed by (tenant, command id) storing a request hash and the outcome, written in the **same transaction** as the state change.
- Same id + same hash → return stored outcome.
- Same id + different hash → reject (409/422): the client reused a key for a different request.
- In progress → 409 with retry-after.
Retention: longer than the client's retry window.

### Validation layers
1. Shape (required fields, formats) at the edge → 400.
2. Reference checks (account exists, currency supported) in the handler → 404/422.
3. Invariants in the aggregate → 409/422 with domain codes.

### Expected version
For edits based on what a user saw: {{ExpectedVersion}} (or If-Match). Mismatch → 412/409 with the current version, so the UI can show changes.

### Useful errors
Stable codes ({{loan.version_conflict}}, {{payment.amount_exceeds_authorised}}), field-level details for validation, and the current version on conflicts.
pts: Client-generated command ids reused on retries.
Idempotency records with request hash in the same transaction.
Three validation layers with distinct status codes.
Expected versions for user edits; return current version on conflicts.
Stable error codes and field details.

questions.q: Security on the read side: denormalised read models copy data from many entities. How do you enforce tenant isolation, per-user permissions and PII rules on read models and search indexes?
questions.a:
### Risks
Read models join data that was protected separately on the write side; a single query endpoint can expose more than any write-side API. Search indexes make it easy to find data across tenants. Copies of PII multiply.

### Controls
- **Tenant id on every read-model row and document**; queries filter by tenant centrally (base query, global filters, database RLS, per-tenant index aliases or filtered aliases in Elasticsearch).
- **Permission-aware projections**: include fields needed for authorization (owner id, branch, visibility flags) so queries can filter; for complex ACLs, precompute visibility sets or use per-user filtered queries.
- **Field-level minimisation**: project only what the screen needs; mask or hash PII (email hash for search, last four digits of card numbers); separate sensitive read models with stricter access.
- **Erasure**: projections must handle deletion/pseudonymisation events (GDPR) across all read models and indexes.
- **Audit** access to sensitive read models.

### Testing
Cross-tenant tests for every query endpoint; automated scans that every read-model table has a tenant column and every query applies the filter.
pts: Read models aggregate data and can over-expose it.
Tenant id everywhere with central filters, RLS and filtered aliases.
Permission fields projected for query-time authorization.
Minimise and mask PII; handle erasure events in every projection.
Cross-tenant tests and automated scans.
questions.ex: A support search index built from payment events had no tenant filter; a support agent of one white-label client could find another client's customers by email. Filtered aliases per tenant and hashed emails closed the exposure.

questions.q: How do you test a CQRS system: command handlers, projections, the integration between them, idempotency and ordering, and end-to-end lag?
questions.a:
### Command side
Given an aggregate state (or events), when a command is handled, then expect events/state changes and the result. Fakes for repositories; real database tests for persistence and outbox.

### Projections
**Given events, then the view**: feed a sequence of events into the projector (in memory or against a containerised read store) and assert the resulting rows/documents. Add cases for:
- **Duplicates** (same event twice → same result).
- **Out of order / gaps** (parked or retried, never corrupt).
- **Rebuild**: replaying all events from scratch yields the same view as incremental application.

### Integration
Command → outbox → broker (Testcontainers Kafka) → projector → read store; assert eventual visibility with a bounded wait (polling helper), never fixed sleeps.

### Contract
Event schemas compatibility tests (schema registry or snapshot tests) so projectors keep working when producers evolve events.

### Non-functional
Load tests measuring projection throughput and lag under realistic event rates; chaos (projector restarts mid-batch) verifying no loss or duplication.
pts: Command tests: given state, when command, then events and result.
Projection tests: given events, then view; include duplicates, gaps, rebuild equivalence.
Integration through outbox and broker with bounded polling, not sleeps.
Event schema compatibility tests.
Load and chaos tests for throughput, lag and loss.
questions.ex: A rebuild-equals-incremental test found that a projector computed refunded amounts differently when events arrived in one batch versus several, a bug that had silently skewed merchant reports after every redeploy.
fu: How do you test eventual consistency without flaky tests?
How do you generate realistic event histories?
What should a projection load test measure?

questions.q: A projection has a bug that corrupted 6 months of data, or its schema must change. Rebuild a read model over billions of events without downtime: blue-green projections, parallelism, verification and cut-over.
questions.a:
### Prerequisites
The source of truth must be replayable: an event store, Kafka topics with sufficient retention or compacted/archived history, or the write database itself (re-derive by scanning). If events are not retained, rebuild from write-side tables via a backfill job.

### Blue-green rebuild
1. Deploy **projector v2** writing to a **new** table/index ({{payments_v2}}), as a new consumer group starting from the beginning (or a snapshot).
2. v1 keeps serving reads.
3. v2 catches up: parallelise by partition, batch writes, disable non-essential indexes during bulk load and recreate after, throttle to protect shared infrastructure.
4. **Verify**: row counts, checksums or sampled comparisons against the source of truth (and against v1 where v1 was correct), business reconciliations (totals per merchant per day).
5. **Cut over** reads via configuration, alias (Elasticsearch alias swap) or view swap; keep v1 for rollback.
6. Retire v1 after a stability window.

### Scale
Billions of events: snapshots or compacted topics as starting points, partition-level parallelism, bulk APIs ({{SqlBulkCopy}}, ES bulk), progress metrics (events/sec, ETA), and capacity planning (rebuilds compete with live traffic).

### Corruption fix without full rebuild
If the bug affected a known subset (one event type, one period), reprocess only affected entities by replaying their streams.

  T1 --> ALIAS{Read alias}
  T2 -. after verification .-> ALIAS
  ALIAS --> Q[Query handlers]

Blue-green: new projector and table, catch up, verify, switch, keep old for rollback.

questions.q: Projection lag is your read side's key health metric. Define it, set SLOs, alert on it, and design for backpressure when a projector falls behind (slow store, poison events, traffic spikes).
questions.a:
### Definitions
- **Time lag**: now − occurred-at of the last applied event (per projection, per partition).
- **Consumer lag**: number of events behind the head of each partition.
- **End-to-end visibility latency**: command commit → visible in the read model (synthetic probe).

### SLOs
Per read model, set by business need: "99% of updates visible within 2 s" for an operational screen; "within 15 minutes" for analytics. Publish them; product and support should know them.

### Alerting
- Lag above threshold for N minutes (warning, then page).
- Consumer lag growing monotonically (falling behind).
- Projector not consuming at all (zero throughput while events exist).
- Lag approaching **retention limits** (data loss risk).

### Backpressure and recovery
- Scale projector instances up to the partition count; increase batch sizes; bulk writes.
- Protect the read store (connection limits, write throttling).
- Isolate poison events (DLQ per entity) so one bad event does not block a partition.
- Prioritise: separate consumer groups for critical vs bulk projections.
- Communicate degraded freshness in the UI ("data as of 10:42") when lag exceeds the SLO.
pts: Track time lag, consumer lag and end-to-end visibility.
SLOs per read model set by business need.
Alert on threshold breaches, growth, stalls and retention risk.
Scale consumers, batch, protect the store, isolate poison events.
Show freshness in the UI when lag exceeds the SLO.
questions.ex: A Black Friday spike pushed a merchant-dashboard projection 25 minutes behind; merchants called support believing payments were lost. Afterwards the team added a freshness banner, separate consumer groups for critical projections and an alert on lag growth, and the next peak stayed within 3 seconds.
fu: How do you measure lag per partition vs per projection?
What freshness indicator would you show to merchants?
How do you prioritise critical projections?
pit: One consumer group for all projections.

questions.q: A malformed or unexpected event makes a projector throw on every retry. Design poison-event handling that protects other entities, preserves ordering where needed, and gets the data fixed.
questions.a:
### Classify failures
- **Transient** (read store unavailable, timeout): retry with backoff; do not advance.
- **Poison** (deserialisation error, unknown enum value, violated assumption, bug in projector): retrying will not help.

### Handling poison events
1. Bounded retries (a few attempts) to rule out transient causes.
2. Move the event to a **dead-letter store** with error details, partition, offset, entity id.
3. **Mark the entity as blocked** in the projection (so later events for the same entity are parked rather than applied out of order), while **other entities continue**.
4. Alert with context (which event type, which entity, error).
5. Fix: deploy a projector fix or data correction, then **replay** the dead-lettered event and the parked successors in order.

### Avoid
- Skipping the event silently (permanent divergence).
- Blocking the entire partition (all entities stall).
- Infinite retry loops consuming resources.

### Prevention
Schema compatibility checks in the producer pipeline, tolerant readers (ignore unknown fields), explicit handling of unknown enum values, and contract tests between producers and projectors.
pts: Separate transient failures (retry) from poison events.
Dead-letter with full context; block only the affected entity.
Park later events for that entity to preserve order.
Alert, fix, then replay dead letters and parked events.
Prevent with schema checks and tolerant readers.
questions.ex: A producer added a new payment status that the projector's enum did not know; the projector crashed-looped and stalled the whole partition, freezing 1/12 of merchant dashboards for two hours. Per-entity blocking with dead-lettering and tolerant enum handling limited the next similar incident to three payments.

What tooling do operators need for DLQs?

questions.q: Events are consumed by 15 projectors owned by different teams. How do you evolve event schemas (additive changes, breaking changes, upcasting during rebuilds) and read-model schemas without breaking anyone?
questions.a:
### Event schema evolution
- **Additive** changes only within a version: new optional fields with defaults; consumers ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader).
- **Breaking** changes (rename, type change, meaning change): new event type or version ({{PaymentCapturedV2}}); publish both during migration; track consumers; retire v1 later.
- **Schema registry** with compatibility mode (backward/full) enforced in producer CI.
- Document semantics, not just shape (is Amount gross or net?).

### Upcasting
During rebuilds, old events in the log still have old shapes. An **upcaster** transforms v1 events to the current version on read (fill defaults, split fields), so projectors only handle the latest version. Keep upcasters tested with stored samples of each historical version.

### Read-model schema changes
- Additive columns: migrate and backfill, or rebuild.
- Structural changes: **blue-green rebuild** into a new table/index and switch.
- API consumers of read models are versioned separately (read-model schema ≠ API contract).

### Governance
Event catalogue with owners and consumers, deprecation policy, consumer registration (who reads what), contract tests between producers and projectors.
pts: Additive changes within a version; tolerant readers.
Breaking changes get new versions published alongside old ones.
Schema registry compatibility checks in producer CI.
Upcasters convert historical events during replays; test with samples.
Read-model schema changes via migration or blue-green rebuild; catalogue and owners.
questions.ex: A producer renamed amount to grossAmount in place; four projectors silently wrote zeros for two days. After introducing a schema registry with backward compatibility and upcasters for old versions, the next breaking change rolled out as v2 with no consumer incidents.
fu: Backward vs forward vs full compatibility: which for events?
How long do you keep publishing v1?
How do you find all consumers of an event?
pit: Projectors handling every historical version ad hoc.

questions.q: A read model needs data from three bounded contexts (payments, customers, merchants). How do you build composite read models from events of several sources, handle different arrival orders and keep them consistent enough?
questions.a:
### Approach: one projector, several event streams
The projector subscribes to events from all three contexts and maintains:
- the **main view** (one row per payment),
- **local lookup tables** for reference data from other contexts (customer display names, merchant names/categories), updated from their events (event-carried state transfer).

### Arrival order across contexts
No ordering guarantee across topics. Handle:
- Payment event arrives before the customer is known → store the row with the customer id and a placeholder; when the customer event arrives, **backfill** rows referencing it (or join at query time from the lookup table).
- Customer renamed → update the lookup; either update denormalised rows (fan-out update) or join at query time if the fan-out is large.

### Join at write vs read
| | Denormalise at projection time | Join at query time |
|---|---|---|
| Query speed | fastest | slower |
| Update cost when reference data changes | fan-out updates (millions of rows) | cheap |
| Good for | rarely changing references | frequently changing references |

### Consistency
Composite views are eventually consistent across sources; expose source versions/timestamps if users need to know. Never rely on composite read models for decisions.
pts: One projector consumes several contexts' events.
Local lookup tables via event-carried state transfer.
Handle cross-source arrival order with placeholders and backfill.
Denormalise rarely changing references; join frequently changing ones at query time.
Composite views are eventually consistent; not for decisions.
questions.ex: A support console joined payments with the customer service via API calls at query time; when the customer service was slow, the console timed out. A composite read model with a local customer lookup fed by events made the console independent of the customer service's availability.

How do you handle a customer deletion event?

pit: Remote calls to other contexts during projection.

questions.q: Feed read models with CDC (Debezium on the write database) or with domain/integration events via an outbox? Compare coupling, semantics, ordering, operations, and when you would combine them.
questions.a:
| | CDC on write tables | Events via outbox |
|---|---|---|
| Semantics | row-level changes ("column Status changed from 2 to 3") | business facts ("PaymentCaptured") |
| Coupling | consumers coupled to **internal table schemas** | consumers coupled to **published contracts** |
| Producer effort | none in application code | events designed and written in each use case |
| Completeness | captures every change, even from scripts and legacy code | only changes that go through code that emits events |
| Ordering | per row / per transaction log order | per aggregate key if designed |
| Schema evolution | table refactors break consumers | contracts versioned independently |
| Operations | Debezium/Kafka Connect, log retention, snapshots | outbox relay |

### Recommendations
- **Within the owning team** (projections of their own data), CDC can be pragmatic: same team owns tables and consumers.
- **Across teams/contexts**, publish **events** (published language); never make other teams depend on your table structure.
- **Outbox + CDC**: use Debezium on the **outbox table** as the relay (no polling, ordered, low latency): business events with CDC mechanics.
- **Legacy systems** that cannot emit events: CDC plus an **anti-corruption translator** that turns row changes into proper events, owned by the legacy system's team.

  DBZ1 --> OWN[Same-team projections only]

CDC couples consumers to tables: acceptable within one team only.

questions.q: Build and operate a search read model (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) for payments and customers: document design, sync from events, mapping changes and reindexing, consistency and relevance.
questions.a:
### Document design
- One document per searchable entity, **denormalised** with fields users search and filter on (references, names, amounts, statuses, dates, tenant).
- Explicit **mappings**: keyword vs text fields, normalisers for case-insensitive exact match, numeric and date types, no dynamic mapping surprises.
- PII minimisation: hashed emails for exact lookup, masked card numbers.

### Sync
- Projector consumes events and uses **external versioning** (aggregate version) so out-of-order or duplicate writes are no-ops.
- Bulk API for throughput; refresh interval tuned (search is near-real-time, about 1 second by default).
- Deletions and erasure events remove or redact documents.

### Mapping changes and reindexing
Mappings cannot be changed in place for existing fields: create **index v2** with the new mapping, rebuild it from events (or reindex API from v1 for simple changes), then **swap the alias**. Keep queries on aliases only.

### Consistency
The index is eventually consistent and may lag or miss documents after failures: run periodic **reconciliation** (counts and checksums per tenant/day against the source), and repair differences.

### Relevance and operations
Analyzers per language, boosting exact reference matches, monitoring of cluster health, shard sizing, and snapshots for disaster recovery.
pts: Denormalised documents with explicit mappings and PII minimisation.
Event-driven sync with external versioning and bulk writes.
Mapping changes via new index, rebuild and alias swap.
Periodic reconciliation against the source to repair drift.
Tune analyzers, refresh, shards and snapshots.
questions.ex: Support agents could not find payments by reference with different casing because the field was mapped as text with the standard analyzer; a v3 index with a lowercase keyword normaliser, rebuilt from events and swapped via alias, fixed search without downtime.

questions.q: Read models vs caching: when is a cache in front of queries enough, when do you need a projected read model, and how do you combine them without staleness bugs?
questions.a:
### Cache in front of queries
- Good when the query is **correct but slow** and data changes rarely relative to reads (reference data, product catalogues, configuration).
- Simple: cache-aside or HybridCache; TTL plus event-based invalidation.
- Problems: cold starts and stampedes, invalidation complexity when results depend on many entities, per-user keys explosion.

### Projected read model
- Good when the query is **structurally expensive** (joins across many tables, aggregations over large data) or must serve **high-volume, low-latency** access patterns regardless of cache hit rates.
- Updated incrementally from events, always "warm".
- Costs: projector infrastructure, rebuilds, lag.

### Combining
- Read models as the source for queries; a short-TTL cache for the hottest keys to reduce read-store load.
- Invalidate caches from the **same events** that update the read model, **after** the read model update (or use version-keyed cache entries).
- Never cache data used for write decisions.

### Decision heuristic
Cache first if a single query is slow and results are reusable. Move to a read model when invalidation becomes complex, misses are expensive, or the shape needs pre-computation.
pts: Cache when a correct query is slow and data changes rarely.
Read models when queries are structurally expensive or must be always warm.
Combine: read models as source, short-TTL cache for hot keys.
Invalidate from the same events after updating the read model, or version keys.
Never cache write-decision data.
questions.ex: A dashboard cache keyed only by merchant id was invalidated before the projection updated; the next request re-cached stale data for 10 minutes. Version-keyed cache entries eliminated the race.

How does HybridCache help across pods?

Complex invalidation instead of a read model.

questions.q: Expose read models to Angular/React front ends: per-screen endpoints, a BFF, or GraphQL over read models? Discuss over/under-fetching, authorization, caching and how commands fit in.
questions.a:
### Options
| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **Per-screen REST endpoints** over read models | simple, cacheable, explicit | many endpoints; front-end changes need backend changes |
| **BFF** (backend for frontend) per client | shapes data for one UI, aggregates several read models/services, handles auth tokens server-side | another deployable; risk of business logic creeping in |
| **GraphQL** over read models | clients choose fields; one round trip for nested data | resolver N+1 (needs DataLoader), complex authorization per field, harder HTTP caching, query cost control |

### Commands
Commands remain explicit operations (REST POST or GraphQL mutations) that map to command handlers, returning ids and versions. Avoid generic "update object" mutations: they lose intent.

### Authorization
Per-field and per-row authorization must be enforced in resolvers or read-model queries, not only at the gateway; GraphQL makes it easy to reach data through unexpected paths.

### Practical choice
For a product UI: a BFF exposing per-screen endpoints backed by read models is usually simplest. GraphQL pays off with many clients and highly variable data needs, with investment in DataLoader, persisted queries and cost limits.
pts: Per-screen endpoints, BFF or GraphQL over read models.
GraphQL needs DataLoader, field-level authorization and cost limits.
Commands stay explicit operations or mutations with intent.
BFFs shape data but must not host business rules.
Choose by number of clients and variability of data needs.

Where should a BFF live organisationally?
How do persisted queries help security?

questions.q: Some commands take seconds to minutes (bulk payouts, statement generation) or must be queued during peaks. Design asynchronous command handling: 202 Accepted, command status resources, queues, retries and client experience.
questions.a:
### Flow
1. API validates the request, assigns a **command id** (or uses the client's idempotency key), stores a **command status** record (Accepted), enqueues the command (outbox → queue), returns **202 Accepted** with a {{Location}} to {{/commands/:id}}.
2. A worker processes the command through the normal handler, updating status (Processing → Succeeded/Failed with reason and result references).
3. Client polls the status resource (with Retry-After), or receives a webhook/push notification.

### Design points
- **Idempotency** across retries of both submission and processing.
- **Validation** split: synchronous shape and permission checks before 202; business validation in the worker (failures reported via status).
- **Progress** for long jobs (processed/total), and cancellation if meaningful.
- **Ordering** per aggregate (partition key) if commands affect the same entity.
- **Priorities**: separate queues for interactive vs bulk commands.
- **Retention** of status records for the client's needs.

### When to use
Long-running work, peak smoothing (queue absorbs bursts), operations requiring external confirmations, batch/bulk operations. Keep normal interactive commands synchronous for simplicity.

questions.q: The read side scales easily, but the write side becomes the bottleneck (hot aggregates, high command rates). How does CQRS help or not help, and how do you scale the command side?
questions.a:
### What CQRS gives the write side
- Writes no longer compete with heavy reads on the same tables and indexes (reads moved to read models/replicas).
- Write models can be **lean**: fewer indexes (only those needed for command lookups and constraints), smaller aggregates.
- Writes can be **asynchronous** (queued commands) to smooth peaks.

### What it does not solve
Contention on hot aggregates and the throughput limits of a single row or partition.

### Scaling the command side
- **Smaller aggregates** sized by invariants; append-only facts instead of updating hot rows (ledger entries rather than balance updates).
- **Sharded counters / sub-aggregates** for hot entities (merchant balance split into N shards).
- **Partitioning commands by aggregate id** so each partition processes sequentially without lock contention (single-writer per key).
- **Batching** commands per aggregate (apply 100 credits in one transaction).
- **Database scaling**: partitioned tables, faster log storage, scale-up; sharding by tenant or key when one database is not enough.
- **Event sourcing** for append-heavy domains (appends are cheap; projections handle reads).

### Measure first
Command latency by type, lock waits, deadlocks, conflict/retry rates per aggregate type, and the hottest keys.
pts: CQRS removes read pressure from write tables and allows lean write models.
It does not fix hot aggregates or partition limits.
Smaller aggregates, append-only facts, sharded counters.
Partition commands by key; batch per aggregate.
Measure conflicts, lock waits and hot keys first.
questions.ex: After moving reports to read models, a payments write database still saturated at month-end because of a merchant balance row updated by every capture. Single-writer partitioning with batched credits raised sustainable throughput from 400 to 6,000 captures per second.

How does event sourcing change write scalability?
How do you find hot keys?
pit: Expecting CQRS to fix write contention.
Retries as the answer to hot rows.

questions.q: Operational read models vs analytical reporting: where do finance reports, regulatory extracts and BI dashboards belong, how do you feed them, and how do you keep numbers consistent with operational screens?
questions.a:
### Two different read sides
| | Operational read models | Analytical store (warehouse/lakehouse) |
|---|---|---|
| Users | customers, agents, operations | finance, risk, management, regulators |
| Latency | seconds | minutes to hours |
| Shape | per screen, current state | facts and dimensions, history |
| Queries | known, indexed | ad hoc, large scans |
| Store | SQL, search, key-value | Snowflake, Databricks, Synapse, BigQuery |

### Feeding analytics
- Stream **integration events** (outbox → Kafka) into the lake (sink connectors), producing fact tables with event history.
- Or CDC from read replicas within the owning team, transformed into curated datasets.
- Domain teams publish **data products** with contracts (see data mesh) rather than a central team scraping databases.

### Consistency between screens and reports
- Define **one authoritative source per metric** (revenue = ledger postings, not payment statuses).
- Reconciliation jobs comparing operational totals with analytical totals and the ledger; alerts on drift.
- Clear **cut-off** definitions (business date vs UTC timestamps; late events).
- Show "as of" timestamps.

### Regulatory extracts
Point-in-time correctness (bitemporal data), reproducibility (versioned transformations), and audit of every extract.

~~~sql
-- Curated fact table built from integration events (lakehouse SQL)
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE finance.fact_captures AS
SELECT e.payment_id, e.merchant_id, CAST(e.captured_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London' AS DATE) AS business_date,
       e.gross_amount, e.fee_amount, e.net_amount, e.currency, e.event_id, e.occurred_at
FROM raw.payments_captured_v2 e
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY e.payment_id ORDER BY e.occurred_at DESC) = 1;   -- dedupe at-least-once delivery

-- Reconciliation: analytics vs ledger per business date
SELECT f.business_date, SUM(f.net_amount) AS analytics_net, l.ledger_net, SUM(f.net_amount) - l.ledger_net AS diff
FROM finance.fact_captures f
JOIN finance.ledger_daily l ON l.business_date = f.business_date
GROUP BY f.business_date, l.ledger_net
HAVING ABS(SUM(f.net_amount) - l.ledger_net) > 0.01;
~~~
pts: Operational read models and analytical stores serve different needs.
Feed analytics from integration events or curated CDC as data products.
One authoritative source per metric, typically the ledger for money.
Reconcile operational, analytical and ledger totals; define cut-offs.
Regulatory extracts need point-in-time correctness and audit.
questions.ex: Merchants saw one revenue figure in the portal and finance another in the monthly pack; the difference came from refunds counted by payment status vs ledger postings and different day cut-offs. Defining the ledger as authoritative and reconciling daily removed the disagreements.

Who owns the analytical data model?
How do you reproduce last year's regulatory extract?

questions.q: Design an account statement / activity timeline read model for 20 million accounts with up to 100,000 entries each: storage layout, pagination, running balances, corrections and performance.
questions.a:
### Model
An **append-only** list of entries per account: entry id, account id, booking date, value date, amount, currency, description, counterparty, running balance, source event id/version.

### Storage
- SQL: table clustered by ({{AccountId}}, {{BookingDate}}, {{EntryId}}) so one account's entries are contiguous; partition by month or hash for maintenance.
- Wide-column / key-value (Cassandra, DynamoDB, Cosmos DB) with account id as partition key and a sort key (date + id) when scale demands.
- Hot recent data in a fast store, older months archived (cheaper storage) but still queryable.

### Pagination
Keyset (booking date + entry id) cursors, newest first; never offset.

### Running balances
Computed at projection time in order per account (single-writer per account), stored with each entry. Back-dated entries (value date in the past) require **recomputation of subsequent balances**: either recompute the tail for that account or show balances by booking order (the convention banks use for statements).

### Corrections
Corrections appear as new entries (reversal + rebook), never edits, matching ledger semantics; the timeline reflects what happened.

### Idempotency and ordering
Unique source event id per entry; per-account ordering by partition key.
pts: Append-only entries clustered by account and date.
Keyset pagination with booking date and entry id.
Running balances computed in order by a single writer per account.
Corrections as reversal entries, matching ledger semantics.
Archive old months; idempotent by source event id.
questions.ex: A neobank's transaction history used offset pagination over a heap table and timed out for business accounts with 300,000 entries. A clustered, keyset-paginated statement read model returned any page in under 10 ms.
fu: How do you handle back-dated postings and running balances?
When would you move this to Cassandra or DynamoDB?
How do you search descriptions efficiently?
pit: Computing running balances at query time over full history.

questions.q: In a banking app, which balances can come from read models and which must come from the authoritative write side? Design the balance displays, holds and available-to-spend calculation with CQRS.
questions.a:
### Authoritative vs projected
| Use | Source |
|---|---|
| **Authorisation decisions** (card auth, transfer approval, overdraft check) | **write side** account aggregate / ledger, consistent |
| Available balance shown on the transfer screen just before confirming | write side (or a read model with version check), because users act on it |
| Balance on the home screen, statements, dashboards | read models (seconds of lag acceptable), with "as of" |
| Analytics, reports | analytical store |

### Available to spend
{{ledger balance − holds (pending card authorisations, reserved payments) + available overdraft}}. Holds are first-class write-side records (authorisation holds created by card auths, released on settlement or expiry). The write side computes available balance atomically for decisions.

### Read models
Projected balances updated from posting and hold events per account (single writer per account), with versions for idempotency, and a freshness timestamp.

### UX
- Show both "balance" and "available" with explanations; pending transactions listed separately.
- After a user's own transfer, show the updated available balance from the command response (read-your-own-writes).

### Reconciliation
Periodic comparison of projected balances with ledger balances; alert on any difference.
pts: Decisions always use the authoritative write side.
Screens users act on immediately read authoritative or version-checked data.
Display balances can come from read models with "as of".
Holds are write-side records; available = ledger − holds + overdraft.
Reconcile projected balances with the ledger.
questions.ex: A card programme authorised purchases against a projected balance that lagged during a batch posting run; customers overspent by a total of 85,000 GBP in two hours. Moving authorisation to the write-side account aggregate with holds eliminated the exposure while the app kept using projected balances for display.
fu: How do holds expire and how is that reflected?
How do you show pending transactions?
What happens if a hold and settlement amounts differ?

questions.q: Push read-model updates to Angular/React clients in real time (payment status, trading blotter): SignalR/WebSockets/SSE design, scaling across pods, authorization, and what to push (deltas vs invalidation signals).
questions.a:
### What to push
- **Invalidation signals** ("payment 123 changed, version 7"): the client re-queries the read model it needs. Simple, secure (authorization reused), resilient to missed messages.
- **Deltas/full objects**: lower latency, fewer requests; must be authorized per recipient, versioned, and the client must handle gaps (re-fetch on version gap).

### Flow
Projector updates the read model → publishes a notification (after commit) → **notification service** fans out to connected clients subscribed to that entity/group (merchant, account, desk).

### Scaling
- SignalR with a **backplane** (Redis) or Azure SignalR Service / managed WebSocket services for many connections.
- Group membership by tenant/merchant/account; never broadcast to all.
- Backpressure: coalesce rapid updates (send latest per entity every 100 ms) for high-frequency data like blotters.

### Authorization
Authenticate the connection (token); authorise group joins server-side (a merchant user can only join their merchant group); re-validate on token expiry.

### Reliability
Clients must assume messages can be lost: on reconnect, re-fetch current state; include versions so clients detect gaps.

### Alternatives
SSE for one-way updates (simpler, HTTP-friendly), polling with ETags for low-frequency updates.
pts: Push invalidation signals (simple, secure) or deltas (fast, more care).
Notify after read-model commit; fan out by authorized groups.
Backplanes or managed services for scale; coalesce high-frequency updates.
Assume lost messages: versions and refetch on reconnect.
SSE or ETag polling as simpler alternatives.
questions.ex: A trading blotter pushed every tick-driven position update to every trader; network and browser CPU saturated during volatility. Coalescing to the latest state per position every 200 ms and pushing only to desk groups cut traffic by 95%.
fu: How do you authorize group membership securely?
When is SSE preferable to SignalR?
How do you load-test real-time fan-out?
pit: Pushing before the read model commits.

questions.q: A customer exercises the right to erasure. Their data is copied into a dozen read models, a search index, caches and the analytics lake, while financial records must be retained for years. Design erasure across a CQRS system.
questions.a:
### Separate what must be retained from what must be erased
Financial records (transactions, ledger entries) are retained under legal obligations, but can be **pseudonymised**: replace personal identifiers with a pseudonymous id; keep the mapping in a separately protected store that can be deleted.

### Erasure as an event
The owning context processes the erasure request (checks legal holds), updates its write model, and publishes **CustomerErased** (or **PersonalDataErased**). Every projector **must handle** it:
- Delete or redact personal fields in read models.
- Delete or update search documents.
- Evict caches.
- Analytics: delete/redact in curated datasets; for immutable lake files, use crypto-shredding or rewrite partitions.

### Crypto-shredding
Encrypt personal data per subject with a key in a key store; deleting the key renders all copies (including event stores and backups) unreadable. Essential for event-sourced systems and immutable logs.

### Verification
- An erasure registry tracking which projections have confirmed processing (consumer acknowledgements).
- Automated checks that searches for the subject return nothing.
- Backups: documented approach (keys deleted, restored data re-erased via the registry).

### Rebuilds
Rebuilt projections must respect erasures (replay applies the CustomerErased event, or source events are already shredded).
pts: Retain financial records pseudonymised; erase personal data.
Erasure is an event every projector must handle.
Search indexes, caches and analytics included.
Crypto-shredding for event stores, logs and backups.
Track confirmations and verify; rebuilds must respect erasures.
questions.ex: An audit found a customer's name and email still searchable in a support index 8 months after an erasure request because that projector ignored the event. A consumer test requiring every projector to handle erasure, plus an erasure registry, made the gap impossible to reintroduce.
fu: How do you reconcile erasure with anti-money-laundering retention?
How do you erase data from Kafka topics?
How do you handle erasure in backups?
pit: Deleting financial records needed by law.

questions.q: Read scaling options: database read replicas, caching, or projected read models in separate stores. Compare consistency, cost and complexity, and decide for a payments portal with 50x more reads than writes.
questions.a:
| Option | Consistency | Effort | Fits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Read replicas** (AG secondaries, Aurora/Azure replicas) | replica lag (ms to seconds), same schema | low: point read-only connections at replicas | same query shapes, more capacity |
| **Caching** (HybridCache, Redis) | TTL/invalidation dependent | low to medium | hot, repeated queries |
| **Projected read models** (same DB or separate stores) | eventual, designed | medium to high | different shapes, expensive queries, search |

### Decision for the portal
1. **Level 1** query handlers with good indexes and projections.
2. Route **read-only** queries to **replicas** ({{ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly}}); keep reads that follow the user's own write on the primary (read-your-own-writes).
3. **Cache** hot reference data and dashboard tiles.
4. Introduce **projected read models** only for screens that remain expensive (merchant analytics, search).

### Replica caveats
Lag spikes under heavy write load or during index maintenance; monitoring replica lag; failover behaviour; licensing costs (SQL Server readable secondaries need licences).

### Principle
Replicas scale capacity for existing query shapes; read models change the shapes. Use the cheaper tool first.
pts: Replicas add capacity for the same query shapes, with replica lag.
Caches for hot repeated queries.
Read models when shapes or costs must change.
Route the user's own recent reads to the primary.
Start with the cheapest tool; monitor replica lag and licence costs.
questions.ex: A payments portal planned a Kafka-fed read store to handle 50x read load; routing read-only queries to an existing Always On secondary and caching dashboard tiles handled the load for a fraction of the effort, leaving projected read models only for full-text search.
fu: How do you detect and handle replica lag spikes?
What happens to read routing during failover?
When do replicas stop being enough?
pit: Separate read stores before trying replicas and caching.
Ignoring replica lag for the user's own writes.

questions.q: Two front-end versions and three partner integrations depend on read-model-backed APIs. How do you evolve read models and their API contracts (new fields, changed semantics, removed screens) without breaking consumers?
questions.a:
### Separate the layers
- **Read-model schema**: internal, owned by the team, changed via migrations or rebuilds.
- **API contract**: external, versioned, documented; mapped from read models.
Changing a read model must not automatically change the API.

### Evolution techniques
- **Additive** API changes in place (new optional fields).
- **Semantic changes** (amount now net instead of gross): new field or new API version; never redefine a field.
- **Multiple read models side by side**: a v2 read model built by a new projector while v1 still serves old clients; both fed by the same events; retire v1 when its consumers move.
- **Sunset headers** and deprecation dates for old API versions; usage metrics per version and per client.
- Front ends: generated clients from OpenAPI; mobile apps need longer support windows (users do not upgrade).

### Partners
Contract tests (consumer-driven) for partner integrations; communication plans; sandbox environments with the new version before cut-over.
pts: Read-model schemas are internal; API contracts are versioned externally.
Additive changes in place; semantic changes via new fields or versions.
Parallel read models fed by the same events during migration.
Sunset headers, usage metrics and longer support for mobile.
Contract tests and sandboxes for partners.
questions.ex: A team changed the amount field in a read model from gross to net and the API followed automatically; a partner's reconciliation broke silently. Decoupling API DTOs from read models and publishing a v2 with explicit gross/fee/net fields avoided repeats.
fu: How long do you support old mobile app versions?
How do you know which partners use v1?
Can GraphQL avoid versioning?
pit: APIs that expose read-model tables directly.
No usage data before retiring versions.

questions.q: A team proposes "full CQRS with separate read stores and Kafka" for a new service. Give your decision framework: when it is worth it, when level 1 suffices, and the questions you ask before approving.
questions.a:
### Questions
1. **Read/write mismatch**: how different are the query shapes from the write model? How many screens, searches, reports?
2. **Load asymmetry**: read volume vs write volume; latency targets.
3. **Technology needs**: full-text search, key-value at extreme scale, analytics?
4. **Consumers outside the context**: do other contexts need the data as read models?
5. **Consistency tolerance**: which screens can lag, by how much? Who agreed?
6. **Team readiness**: experience with eventual consistency, projections, rebuilds, operations of brokers and extra stores?
7. **Lifetime and complexity** of the domain.

### Guidance
| Situation | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| CRUD, few screens | no CQRS; plain EF Core |
| Rich domain, normal query load | **level 1**: separate query handlers, projections, indexes |
| Some expensive aggregations, immediate consistency needed | **level 2**: synchronous projections, indexed/materialised views |
| Search, extreme read scale, cross-context consumers, accepted lag | **level 3** for those read models only |

### Approval conditions for level 3
Lag SLOs agreed with product, idempotent/ordered projectors, rebuild tooling, lag monitoring and alerts, poison-event handling, ownership and on-call for each store, and a plan for erasure and schema evolution.
questions.code:
~~~text
Architecture review checklist: CQRS level 3 proposal

[ ] Query inventory: 23 screens; 3 cannot meet p95 with level 1 (evidence: Query Store, load test)
[ ] Search requirement: free-text over payments by reference/email (needs search engine)
[ ] Lag SLO agreed with product: dashboards 5 s p99, search 30 s p99
[ ] Projectors: idempotent (versions), ordered (partition by payment id), checkpoints atomic
[ ] Rebuild: blue-green tooling, Kafka retention 13 months + archive
[ ] Monitoring: lag metrics, synthetic freshness probe, alerts routed to owning team
[ ] Poison events: per-entity DLQ, replay tooling
[ ] GDPR: every projector handles PersonalDataErased
[ ] Ownership: team-payments owns Elasticsearch cluster runbook and on-call
Decision: approve level 3 for search + dashboards only; remaining 20 screens stay level 1
~~~
